transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-08 07:00 PT / 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~47m
Recording: (fireflies link omitted)
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood Product), Jonah Park (NexaRetail Platform Lead), Maya Gupta (NexaRetail SRE), Ethan Li (NexaRetail ML), Sara Cole (NexaRetail Product)
Shared artifacts: quick deck (shared), sample prompt-pack (s3 link), ops histogram (sheet link)

Summary (auto-ish):
Redwood team walked through an edge-case focused demo: long context preservation across multi-turn sessions (~200k token history), behavior under sudden TPS surges (multi-tenanted retail peak), and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Showed Console telemetry for KV cache hits, per-token latency heatmaps, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization. Customer asked about KV eviction policies, graceful degradation (model fallback and truncated-history responses), TLS/KMS, and Dedicated vs Hosted thresholds. Agreed to run a small on-prem pilot and exchange traffic histograms + prompt sets.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, um we know NexaRetail's peak windows are tricky so today we're going to do a targeted playthrough focusing on long-history sessions, high TPS surges, and how streaming behaves when backpressure kicks in. Priya will drive the demo and Marco will jump in on product tradeoffs.
[00:00:18] Jonah (NexaRetail): thanks Alex. quick context — our checkout assistant holds user session transcripts for up to, like, 150k tokens because customers sometimes paste receipts and long chats. Peak transactions hit ~14k RPS across regions for us during promos. so curious how you deal with history memory and if streaming will stall or time out.
[00:00:40] Priya (Redwood): got it. quick plan: 1) show API with a long-session prompt chain and KV cache mechanics, 2) simulate TPS surge and show autoscale/fallbacks, 3) induce streaming backpressure and show graceful fallbacks and console traces.
[00:00:56] Maya (NexaRetail): we also need to see audit logs and KMS encryption in action — can't expose PII.
[00:01:05] Marco (Redwood): we'll touch on that in the security appendix, but short answer: you can tie keys to customer KMS and we emit audit logs with request hashes, not raw payloads, for on-prem options.
[00:01:20] Priya (Redwood): i'm sharing my screen — starting with a synthetic session: initial prompt + 40 turns of user and assistant. note the KV cache: we set prefix caching on the first 120k tokens and a rolling window afterwards.
[00:01:42] [00:01:50] Speaker 2: (background noise)
[00:01:55] Priya: okay so here is the call to /v1/generate with request headers, you can see token_count ~128k in metadata; runtime returns a 200 and a stream with chunked SSEs. i'm toggling a flag to force a forced miss on the KV to show the cold path.
[00:02:20] Ethan (NexaRetail): quick question — when the KV misses, do you re-append the full prefix to the prompt or do you rely on model stitching? we've seen blowups in latency when prefix rehydration occurs.
[00:02:34] Priya: great point. our runtime recomputes the minimal delta — we avoid re-sending the entire prefix; instead we reconstruct the minimal KV pages needed. The console trace shows the delta size here — see the spike at 00:02:40 where latency increases by ~180ms per token.
[00:02:55] Jonah: that 180ms — is that predictable? our SLO is 500ms p95 for interactive flows.
[00:03:04] Priya: in this setup yes but depends on model size and quantization — Optimize suggests using int8-quant for tail tokens to shave ~80ms. also batching policies can reduce per-token cost but add latency; we'll demo an adaptive policy.
[00:03:20] Alex: i'm going to flip the traffic generator to simulate your 1-min promo window — ramp to 14k RPS across two regions. watch the Console for per-route latencies and the routing fallback that kicks in.
[00:03:34] [00:04:05] (simulated loadnoise)
[00:04:06] Priya: okay load's on — autoscaler registers queue depth up and starts provisioning Dedicated burst nodes. you can see a few requests get routed to the cheaper hosted variant to keep latency for high-priority routes.
[00:04:24] Maya: routed to hosted — but we require all PII to remain in our VPC — does that imply those routed requests expose data?
[00:04:33] Marco: good callout. the policy here was 'latency-first' not 'vpc-only'. in production you can set routing policies like region/policy: 'isolation-first' which will avoid routing off VPC/private instances. the demo used a permissive policy to show graceful fallbacks.
[00:04:49] Jonah: can we see what happens when streaming stalls? we tend to see clients time out after 10s and then retry which doubles TPS.
[00:04:58] Priya: yes — inducing backpressure now. i'm going to artificially cap the streamer buffer on one node so SSEs slow down.
[00:05:12] [00:05:20] Priya: console: look at the stream_health panel — you can see the drop in chunk rate and the backlog metric climbing. at ~00:05:30 we hit the stream timeout threshold for some clients; Redwood's runtime emits a 'stream-shedding' event and replaces the stream with a short fallback response citing 'partial response served' so the client gets something instead of hanging.
[00:05:40] Ethan: partial responses are ok but we need deterministic behavior for our post-processing. can we configure guaranteed termination tokens or a structured 'incomplete' wrapper so our downstream doesn't parse broken JSON?
[00:05:54] Priya: yes you can opt in for structured fallback envelopes — the SDK will emit a JSON wrapper with metadata: {status:partial, tokens_served, fallback_model}. i'll attach the sample envelope. (note: envelope excerpt displayed, transcription may garble braces)
[00:06:10] Jonah: great. what about retransmits — when client retries it ups load; do you have idempotency or dedupe for quickly retried completions?
[00:06:20] Alex: we have request-id idempotency for 60s windows; the runtime can detect duplicate request signatures and return the cached response or a status that tells the client to hydrate locally. that reduces double-execution on surge.
[00:06:35] Maya: what about KV eviction heuristics — we can't afford to lose session context mid-checkout.
[00:06:42] Priya: two levers: soft TTL-based page eviction and LRU by access frequency; plus we expose a prioritized pinning API so you can mark critical sessions as 'pinned' during transaction windows. pinned pages cost more but we keep them in memory. I'll show the Optimize tab recommending pin thresholds based on your heatmap.
[00:06:58] [00:07:30] Priya: opening the Optimize console — here's a suggested profile: 60% pinned during peak, burst capacity at 1.5x baseline, int8 quant for assistant tail. it estimates cost increase vs. p95 latency improvements.
[00:07:48] Ethan: curious about quality regressions with quant — can Optimize run a prompt-set eval to show expected delta?
[00:07:56] Marco: yes we bake evals into rollouts — you can surface BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics or task-specific scoring. we also have regression alerts tied to labeled prompt sets for guardrails.
[00:08:10] [00:08:30] Priya: next test — high concurrency with many long sessions concurrently to force KV churn. watch the eviction_rate metric. sending 4k concurrent long-sessions.
[00:08:45] [00:09:20] (sim load)
[00:09:23] Priya: eviction_rate spiking. you can see some sessions get truncated; we configured truncate-policy: 'keep-last-n-turns' which preserves the last 2 turns but drops older history.
[00:09:36] Jonah: that truncation causes context loss for upsell logic; can we instead stitch with summary tokens so the model keeps important state?
[00:09:44] Priya: earlier we mentioned 'summary compaction' — runtime can optionally run a cheap summarizer pass to compress older history into a 256-token summary which stays in KV. this reduces token footprint while keeping semantically important bits. it is an async op and may add small CPU overhead.
[00:09:58] Maya: do we get audit trails for these summarizer ops? need compliance.
[00:10:05] Marco: yes, each compaction is logged with a hash and retention link. the content itself can be redacted at write-time per KMS policies.
[00:10:18] [00:10:40] Jonah: okay let's simulate client timeouts and retry storms — we saw doubling of TPS because of naive retries.
[00:10:48] Priya: toggling retry guards in the SDK: client-side jitter/backoff reduces retry amplification. plus you can set a 'retry-policy' at the route level — here we set it to exponential with 3 attempts.
[00:11:06] Alex: also note our Console shows 'amplification events' builders — you get a waterfall view of retries and their parent requests so you can tune clients.
[00:11:18] Ethan: regarding private deployment: how different is behavior on a VPC Dedicated box vs hosted — do backpressure modes differ?
[00:11:28] Priya: behavior is the same runtime, but control-plane routing and burst policies differ. on-hosted we have more headroom to spill to compatible model variants in other regions. on Dedicated/VPC you control allowed fallbacks, so if you prohibit spill it may trigger queueing or 503s depending on policy.
[00:11:47] Maya: so for our compliance we probably need 'no-spill' — but that means we need higher reserve capacity. can you show cost tradeoffs?
[00:11:55] Marco: switching to the pricing compare in Console — here's Dedicated with 2x reserve vs Hosted spillage. cost delta shown, plus the SLA difference. I'll share the export.
[00:12:10] Jonah: what's the minimal Dedicated capacity to hit our 500ms p95 during promos without spill?
[00:12:18] Priya: ballpark: based on your histogram, ~40 gpus reserved with n-scheduler tuning; Optimize has a 'capacity calculator' that I can run with your exact percentiles once you share the histogram.
[00:12:30] [00:12:50] (small pause)
[00:12:55] Priya: now — a subtle edge: streaming chunk ordering during partial reconnects. I'm going to kill one of the stream workers to simulate node flaps. you may see out-of-order chunks on some clients.
[00:13:10] Ethan: we observed that in our integration; we ended up implementing sequence ids to reorder. do you support seq ids?
[00:13:18] Priya: yes SSE chunks include sequence metadata and a commit token; SDKs will do reorder and dedupe. the runtime may also compress small deltas into single larger SSEs if network jitter is high.
[00:13:30] Jonah: all right — show us the worst-case where a long session sees both KV eviction and stream timeout at the same time.
[00:13:38] Priya: right now turning on simultaneous eviction rule and forcing stream buffer to low.
[00:13:55] [00:14:20] (beeping from sim)
[00:14:22] Priya: you can see a few requests returned with 'partial envelope' plus a suggested retry-window header. the Console generated an incident with correlation id; clicking into it shows stack traces and the eviction events that coincided.
[00:14:40] Maya: this is useful. how fast can we triage in our SRE runbooks?
[00:14:46] Alex: we can pre-populate runbooks in your Console workspace — including step-by-step mitigation: pin, scale, change routing policy, or enable summary compaction. we'll export as markdown.
[00:14:58] [00:15:25] Marco: quick note re: fallbacks — when streaming fails, we prefer returning a smaller deterministic assistant response from a lower-cost model to keep UX consistent. that's why Optimize suggests a policy of 'model-fallback-first' for checkout routes.
[00:15:40] Jonah: what's the risk of hallucination with compressed summaries? we can't have incorrect order confirmations.
[00:15:48] Priya: summary compaction uses conservative extractive summary models by default; plus you can add verification steps where we run a validation prompt to cross-check salient fields. those validators can be cheap small models.
[00:16:02] Ethan: about telemetry — can we get token-level traces for a given request id? we need to audit why a particular suggestion was generated.
[00:16:10] Marco: yes token-level traces are available but redacted by default; you can request full traces for a short window with appropriate KMS permissions. logs are retained per your retention policy.
[00:16:26] [00:16:50] Maya: can we run the pilot on-prem? our security team prefers air-gapped tests first.
[00:16:58] Alex: we support on-prem packages and a private control plane. pilot would be a small Dedicated cluster with restricted egress; we'll need to schedule a 2-hour install window.
[00:17:10] Jonah: timeline-wise — we want to start next month. what's the gate for enabling burst on Dedicated — is it a config flip or contract?
[00:17:19] Marco: burst capacity requires either pre-approved burst credit or a short-term override; for pilots we usually enable a temporary burst so you can test in real traffic. we'll follow up with contract language.
[00:17:30] [00:17:53] Priya: last demo piece: handing long-sessions to reranker/fallback pipelines to reduce tokens. showing 'local rerank' where we send an embedding-based compacted candidate set to a smaller model — reduces the long-history attention blowup.
[00:18:12] Ethan: embedding cost — are embeddings charged separately in your billing?
[00:18:17] Alex: yes per-embedding units; Optimize may recommend caching common embeddings and deduping. we'll show cost estimates in the export.
[00:18:30] [00:19:00] (discussion on pricing specifics, briefly garbled)
[00:19:20] Priya: wrapping up with a live failure scenario: i induce a 10s network pause in one region, then restart. look at client retries, dedupe and the stream reorder recovery.
[00:19:40] [00:20:05] (simulated pause)
[00:20:10] Priya: region recovers; SDK rehydrates using commit tokens and requests the missing chunk range — no full re-execution required.
[00:20:22] Jonah: that commit token flow looks solid. we'll need to test with our mobile clients which have intermittent networks.
[00:20:30] Alex: noted; we'll include mobile SDK best practices.
[00:20:40] Maya: small ops question — how to surface the pinning API? REST or Console?
[00:20:47] Priya: both. REST call: POST /v1/sessions/{id}/pin with priority, and a Console toggle for manual pin during incident windows.
[00:20:58] Jonah: okay — quick recap?
[00:21:05] Alex: recap: 1) KV cache + summary compaction reduce token footprint and help long-history, 2) pinning for critical sessions, 3) autoscale + routing policies for surge control, 4) streaming: sequence ids, commit tokens, partial envelope for graceful degradation, 5) Optimize suggests quant/batching/capacity profiles and runs evals to detect quality regressions.
[00:21:32] Marco: deliverables: benchmark harness + sample prompts, security packet, pricing export for Dedicated with burst, install window options.
[00:21:44] Jonah: and next step we agreed to pilot — NexaRetail will share histograms and prompt packs by next Friday.
[00:21:52] Alex: perfect — any remaining questions?
[00:22:00] Sara (NexaRetail): only one — how do we avoid accidental spill during incident testing?
[00:22:06] Marco: we'll provide a test tenant with routing policy pre-set to 'isolation-only' and show a 'no-spill' smoke test.
[00:22:15] Jonah: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[00:22:20] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts in the thread.

(end of transcript)

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings; placeholders for deck/links. This call emphasized operational mitigations: pinning, summary compaction, idempotency, structured partial envelopes, and Console-driven runbooks. Agreed pilot + deliverables listed above.
